Procastino

Designing for the moment your brain says nap and the deadline says no.

Procastino is a smart productivity chair with a companion app. Your phone goes into a box behind the chair, focus music and gentle vibrations keep you working, and the reward, a massage and a message in a loved one's voice, only comes once the task is done.

Role
UX Designer & Interaction Designer
Timeline
3 weeks
Designed for
One user, Anukampa
Tools used
Interviews, empathy mapping, Crazy 8, sketching, paper prototyping

01 Chapter one

The context — five techniques, none of them stuck.

Anukampa is 23 and a master's student in design. Her days have structure: up at 7:30, college until 4:30. Her evenings don't. They drift between naps, going out, the gym and assignments pushed toward an 11pm–12am bedtime. She wasn't short of methods.

  1. 01Pomodoro technique
  2. 02Reminders
  3. 03Tracking her work
  4. 04Tidying her desk
  5. 05Music to focus
…and still ended up working spontaneously, despite the checklist.From the research poster Evidence

The problem wasn't that she lacked tools. None of them could survive contact with her real life, so another technique wasn't going to help. My reading

02 Research method

Interview.

One person, interviewed in depth. The final interview guide had eight sections, moving from easy questions about her day to how she feels when work slips, and the gap between her ideal day and her real one.

Final interview guide

Each section opened with an easy question, then went deeper into habits, triggers and feelings. One example question per section is shown.

Evidence
  1. IntroductionYour name, age, and where you currently live?
  2. Warm-upCan you walk me through what a typical day looks like for you?
  3. Focus & productivityHas your definition of productivity changed over time?
  4. PatternsWhat conditions lead to a more, and a less, productive day?
  5. Motivation & breaksHow easy is it for you to get back to work after a break?
  6. Time & contextIf you had full control over your schedule, how would you structure your day?
  7. Reality vs expectationWhat would your ideal work environment look like? How close is it to your current one?
  8. ClosingAnything else you would like to add?
03 Synthesis

What the conversation revealed.

I mapped everything she told me onto one poster: goals, routine, environment, distractions, working style, techniques and motivation. Tap a marker to read it.

Evidence

Her phone was the main enemy.

Notifications pulled her away, and even without them there was the urge to pick it up.

Evidence

Fear was doing all the work.

Fear of failing a course, missing a deadline or disappointing people got her working, and only under tight deadlines. Underneath, she wanted to do her best.

Evidence

Her space was working against her.

Her ideal place had sunlight, good light and tidiness. Her real one was cluttered and dimly lit.

My reading

Willpower-based systems kept failing.

Every technique she'd tried depended on her choosing to follow it, in the moment, every time.

04 Defining the opportunity

Turning findings into principles.

Each finding became a rule the design had to follow. The features appear in my project; the reasoning in the middle column is mine, made explicit here. My reading

What I sawWhat it meantWhat I designed for
SawShe reaches for her phone without deciding to
MeantWillpower loses to habit
DesignedTake the phone away physically
SawFear gets her working, but only at the last minute
MeantFear works, but it's exhausting
DesignedReplace fear with a reward to work toward
SawShe wants to do her best
MeantThere's a positive motivation underneath
DesignedMake encouragement personal, in a voice she trusts
SawEvery technique relied on her choosing to follow it
MeantThe system has to start itself
DesignedOne action starts the session: put the phone away
SawHer environment is dim and cluttered
MeantHer surroundings drain focus
DesignedControl what she hears and feels while working
All five shapeProcastino

The difference is one word. Not a tip, not an app, not a habit to remember: something that holds the structure for her.

05 Ideation

Crazy 8's.

To avoid falling in love with my first idea I used Crazy 8: fold a page into eight panels and sketch eight ideas in eight minutes. I ran it four to five times, pushing a different angle each round. Evidence

Concept 1

The Voice Button

Press it and hear someone you love, your mother or a close friend, encouraging you. It aimed straight at the positive motivation she already had.

Carried into the chair: the loved one's voice

Concept 2

FocusTune headphones

Set a timer for a task. Focus music plays and only stops when the task is done, so the end of the music signals finishing.

Carried into the chair: focus music and the task timer

Concept 3

The Bubble Pod

A full enclosure: focus music, lighting that adjusts to your mood and vitals, a projector showing your ideal future, the voice, and a massage chair with posture sensors.

Carried into the chair: sensors and massage

06 Critique & iteration

The note that changed everything.

I put all three concepts in front of my class. People loved the voice idea, and the Bubble Pod got the most excitement. Then two separate notes asked the question I hadn't.

"Seems very relaxing… it might be a bit too relaxing, as it might put me to sleep."Classmate, on the Bubble Pod · Evidence
"Does this idea lead to intrinsic motivation, or a total relaxation?"Classmate, on the Bubble Pod · Evidence
"Think about something that will help me get started."Classmate, on all concepts · Evidence

They were right. The Pod was so comfortable it risked becoming the nap it was meant to prevent.

Comfort shouldn't be the environment. It should be the reward.

My reading Your project shows this change; the reasoning is stated here for the first time.

From the Voice Button

  • Loved one's recorded voice

From FocusTune

  • Focus music
  • Task timer

From the Bubble Pod

  • Sensors
  • Massage
  • Enclosure
  • Projector of your ideal future
  • Mood-sensing lighting
Rebuilt intoOne chair, smaller and more honest.
07 The product

Meet Procastino.

A smart productivity chair with a companion app. Your phone goes into the Focus Box behind the chair, and it only unlocks when the task is complete.

  • 1
    SpeakersPlay your focus music, and the voice message at the end.
  • 2
    Vibration & massage pointsGentle vibrations keep you alert during the session. Pressure points along the back are designed to support mood and motivation; the physiological effect hasn't been tested.
  • 3
    Focus BoxBehind the chair. Your phone goes in, the timer starts, and it unlocks when the task is done.
  • 4
    ReclineEvery 30 minutes the app suggests a micro-break. Accept and the chair reclines for 30 seconds.
Show the micro-break recline
Redrawn from my sketch

Proportions are indicative. The numbered markers match the list.

  1. Set upConnect the chair to the app and record, or upload, a message in a loved one's voice.
  2. ChoosePick a focus mode (Light, Deep or Hyper Focus), set a timer, choose a soundtrack.
  3. Let goPut the phone in the Focus Box. That single action is the switch that starts the session.
  4. Stay presentGentle vibrations keep her alert. Every 30 minutes, the app suggests a 30-second reclining break.
  5. Earn itWhen the task is complete: a gentle massage, and her mother's voice telling her she did it.

11 Validation & feedback

Usability testing.

I built a physical prototype: a chair cover marking the sensor points, an annotated product drawing, the paper app and an exhibition poster. Then I tested it.

12People tested it
3Changes it pointed to
Evidence

When people heard the message in Anukampa's mother's voice, they smiled.

I hadn't predicted that one personal detail would carry so much weight. It was the clearest sign that personal encouragement, not more features, is the heart of the product.

Feedback

"Make it portable." Something you attach to any chair, cheaper and more accessible than buying a whole chair.

Next

A portable attachment: the Focus Box, speakers and vibration pad as a kit for the chair you already own.

Feedback

"Put a screen on the chair." Plug in and set up while sitting down, with no app.

Next

On-chair controls. This also solves a gap in the current design: once the phone is in the box, the app can't show anything during the session.

Feedback

"What if there's an emergency?" How do you take an important call while the phone is locked away during the massage?

Next

An emergency release for the Focus Box, designed so it isn't an easy escape from the session.

12 Reflection

What I'm taking with me.

Design is the idea, not the drawing.

I came in believing designers had to be excellent illustrators and masters of every tool. This project showed me the concept, and the thinking behind it, is what makes the work strong.

Empathy is the material.

The most powerful feature came from understanding one person's motivation, not from adding technology.

Speed protects you from your first idea.

Crazy 8 forced me past the obvious and kept me from overcomplicating things.

Simple goes further.

The Bubble Pod had everything. The chair works better because it has less.

What I'd do differently
  • Test with Anukampa herself over several real work sessions, not only in a demo setting.
  • Design what happens when someone stops a session early.
  • Check whether the massage reward stays motivating once it's no longer new.
  • Validate the pressure-point claim, or present it only as an intended effect.

I didn't give her another technique. I gave her a reason to finish: a place where the phone disappears, the work gets done, and the reward is her mother's voice telling her she did it.
